value.overview: The Surfbird (Calidris virgata) is a stocky shorebird named for its habit of feeding in the spray zone of rocky ocean coasts. It breeds in remote, rocky alpine tundra in northwestern North America and spends the nonbreeding season mainly along Pacific coastlines from Alaska to southern South America. Unlike many sandpipers, it is strongly associated with wave-washed rocks, where it searches for small marine invertebrates and other shoreline food.
value.classification: The Surfbird belongs to the sandpiper family Scolopacidae and the shorebird order Charadriiformes. Its scientific name is Calidris virgata.
value.identification: A Surfbird is a compact, short-legged shorebird with a short, blunt bill, usually showing an orange or yellowish base to the bill and dull yellow legs. Nonbreeding adults are mostly slate-gray above with a pale belly and finely marked breast. Breeding birds are more heavily spotted below and may show rusty tones on the back and wings. In flight, look for a pale wing stripe and a contrasting black-and-white tail pattern.
value.rangeHabitat: Surfbirds breed in rocky alpine tundra of Alaska and western Canada, often among scree, lichens, dwarf shrubs, and low tundra vegetation. Outside the breeding season they use rocky marine shorelines, wave-cut platforms, jetties, and occasionally sandy beaches or estuaries. In Costa Rica, the species occurs mainly as an uncommon migrant and winter visitor on suitable Pacific coastal habitats, especially rocky shorelines. It is not a breeding species there and is generally localized rather than widespread inland.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant, the Surfbird moves from Arctic and subarctic breeding grounds to Pacific coastal areas in autumn and returns north in spring. In Costa Rica it is a nonbreeding visitor, usually encountered during migration or the boreal winter, primarily along the Pacific coast.
value.breeding: Surfbirds nest in remote alpine environments, often at high elevations above or near the treeline. The nest is a shallow depression on rocky ground, lined with moss, lichens, leaves, or other plant material. The female usually lays four eggs. Both adults participate in incubation and care for the precocial young. Breeding pairs are relatively dispersed, although the species is more social than many other shorebirds outside the breeding season.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small marine invertebrates, including amphipods, insects, mollusks, crustaceans, and other organisms living among rocks and seaweed. Surfbirds also take fish eggs and other concentrated shoreline foods when available. They forage by walking and probing among wave-washed stones, often feeding close to breaking surf. Their short bill is well suited to picking prey from rock surfaces and crevices.
value.behavior: Surfbirds are active, alert shorebirds that commonly forage in flocks, sometimes with Black Turnstones and other coastal waders. They tolerate heavy surf and move quickly across slippery rocks while avoiding incoming waves. Individuals may chase smaller shorebirds from rich feeding spots, particularly where food is concentrated. When disturbed, flocks often fly low along the shoreline, showing their bold wing and tail patterns before settling again on rocks or beaches.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is considered to be declining overall, although the magnitude and pattern of change vary among regions and monitoring programs.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include disturbance and degradation of coastal feeding areas, pollution, changing marine food supplies, climate-related changes affecting both Arctic breeding grounds and coastal wintering sites, and disturbance or predation at remote breeding locations. Because Surfbirds depend heavily on rocky shorelines, localized coastal development and intensive recreation can reduce access to feeding habitat.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect rocky shores, intertidal habitats, and other coastal areas used by migrating and wintering shorebirds. Keep dogs under control, avoid flushing feeding flocks, reduce litter and pollution, and support protected coastal areas and long-term shorebird monitoring. In Costa Rica, careful observation of Pacific shoreline birds and reporting sightings to reputable bird-monitoring programs can improve knowledge of this uncommon visitor.
